0.title: Judgment and Hell
0.essay:
Few Christian teachings are harder to speak about than judgment and hell. Many believers quietly hope the subject will not come up, at the dinner table, in the office, or in their own thoughts at three in the morning. Yet the Lord Jesus spoke of it often and plainly, and he spoke of it with tears in his eyes.

A subject we would rather avoid

Our reluctance is understandable. Hell has been preached with harshness and even with relish. It has been used to frighten children and to control the vulnerable. Many of our friends think the very idea is cruel, and some of us half agree with them. So we stay silent, or we soften the words until they mean very little.

But silence is not kindness. If a doctor sees a shadow on the scan, the loving thing is to say so, gently and clearly, and then to speak of the cure. Scripture does exactly that. It tells us the truth about the judgment we face, and in the same breath it tells us of a mercy that is greater still: “Whoever believes in him is not condemned” (John 3:18).

What this study does

This study asks why judgment troubles us, who the Judge is, what Jesus actually taught, where faithful Christians have disagreed, and whether it is fair. Then it comes to the centre: the cross, where judgment fell on the Judge himself. It ends with how to live, love and grieve in the light of that day. It tries to meet hard questions honestly and to speak with tenderness, because this is a subject for trembling, not for point-scoring.

Several studies sit close by. The Attributes of God (Righteous and Wrathful) explains God’s justice and wrath; Death, Dying & Heaven looks at death and the life to come; End Times Models sets out the order of the last things; and The Person & Work of Christ explains the cross more fully.

The chapters

Why We Struggle with Judgment; The Judge of All the Earth; What Jesus Taught About Hell; Where Christians Differ; Is It Fair?; The Cross: Judgment Taken for Us; and Living in the Light of Judgment.

For reflection

When the subject of hell comes up, what do you feel first: fear, embarrassment, anger, sorrow, or something else? Why do you think that is?

1.title: Why We Struggle with Judgment
1.essay:
Many people today can believe in a God of love. A God who judges is another matter. To modern ears the idea sounds primitive, harsh, even dangerous. Before we look at what Scripture says, it is worth asking honestly why we react as we do, and whether a world without judgment would really be the kinder place we imagine.

Our modern instincts

Several instincts shape us. The first is that judging is the great sin of our age. “Who are you to judge?” closes many conversations. The second is that we picture God as a kind of patient therapist, there to affirm us, not to call us to account. The third is that we struggle to believe that anything we have done could be serious enough to matter eternally. Most of us are, we think, fairly decent people. And the fourth is that we have seen religion used to terrify people into obedience, and we want nothing to do with it.

Some of this deserves a hearing. Christians have at times spoken of hell with an anger that looked more like contempt than love. Jesus did not. When he looked at Jerusalem, the city that would reject him and fall under judgment, “he wept over it” (Luke 19:41). Any talk of judgment that has no tears in it has not learned from him.

Is a world without judgment kinder?

Yet imagine a universe with no final judgment. The man who trafficked girls across borders and died rich and unpunished simply got away with it. The dictator who emptied villages never answers for it. The quiet abuser whom no one believed is never exposed. In such a world, the deepest wrongs of history are never put right. They are simply forgotten.

That is not a kinder world. It is a world in which victims are told that what was done to them does not finally matter. The Bible will not say that. The martyrs in Revelation cry out, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10). And the psalms call the whole creation to sing at the thought of God’s coming as Judge: “Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth” (Psalm 96:12–13). In Scripture, judgment is not only something to fear. It is something the wronged long for.

What a theologian from a war zone saw

Miroslav Volf is a Croatian theologian who watched his homeland torn apart by the wars in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s. In his book Exclusion and Embrace he argued, against the grain of much Western thought, that belief in a God who will finally judge does not feed human violence. It is the very thing that makes it possible to give violence up. If no one will ever put things right, the victim is tempted to take vengeance himself. If God will judge, the victim can lay down the sword. Volf suggested that the idea of a God who never judges is born in quiet, comfortable places, and that it does not survive in a land soaked in the blood of the innocent.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that this is exactly Paul’s logic. “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). The command not to repay evil for evil rests on the promise that God will deal with evil himself. Take away the Judge, and you have not made people gentler. You have only made them responsible for justice, with no power to bring it about.

The difficulty underneath

If we are honest, our real objection is not usually to judgment as such. We want God to judge the trafficker and the tyrant. What troubles us is the thought that he might judge us. Paul saw this long ago: “Do you suppose, O man… that you will escape the judgment of God?” (Romans 2:3). Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, who survived the Soviet labour camps, observed that the line between good and evil does not run between nations or parties but through every human heart. It runs through ours.

That is why the Bible’s message about judgment is never only bad news. We need a Judge who will put the world right. We also need a Saviour, because when the world is put right, we are among the things that need putting right. The astonishing claim of the gospel, which this study will reach in chapter 6, is that the Judge and the Saviour are the same person.

An example

In a university discussion group, a student says the idea of divine judgment is barbaric and belongs in the past. A woman from another country, older than the rest, has been quiet all evening. She says softly that soldiers burned her village when she was a girl and that no one was ever tried. “If there is no judgment,” she says, “then what they did does not matter. I cannot believe that.” The room goes still. Then she adds that she has had to learn something harder: that she too needs mercy. Judgment, for her, is not a cruel idea. It is part of her hope.

For reflection

Which of the modern instincts described here do you recognise in yourself? Why might belief in a God who judges help us not to take revenge? Is there a wrong in the world, or in your own life, that you long to see put right? Do you find it easier to want judgment for others than for yourself?

2.title: The Judge of All the Earth
2.essay:
When the Bible first calls God “the Judge of all the earth”, the words come from a man pleading for mercy. That is worth noticing. Abraham did not fear that God’s justice would be too harsh. He was sure it would be right, and he built his prayer on it.

Abraham’s question

The Lord told Abraham that the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah had reached him. God did not act on rumour. “I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me” (Genesis 18:21). Abraham, whose nephew Lot lived in Sodom, then drew near and asked, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25).

It is one of the great questions of the Bible, and the answer is yes. Abraham did not have to make God more just than he is. He appealed to the justice God already has. Every prayer for justice in a broken world, every cry of a wronged person in the night, stands on that question. The Attributes of God (Righteous and Wrathful) explores God’s justice and wrath more fully; here we ask what kind of Judge he is.

Justice as part of his goodness

We sometimes imagine that God is loving on his good days and just on his bad ones. Scripture does not divide him like that. His justice is part of his goodness. “The LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice, and he judges the world with righteousness” (Psalm 9:7–8). Isaiah can even say, “the LORD waits to be gracious to you… For the LORD is a God of justice” (Isaiah 30:18). Grace and justice are spoken in the same breath.

A good parent is angry when a child is bullied. A good doctor hates the cancer. A good God cannot be neutral about evil, because evil destroys what he loves. His judgment is not a fit of temper. It is his goodness meeting what ruins his world and his creatures.

What kind of Judge he is

Human courts do their best, but they make mistakes. Witnesses lie, evidence goes missing, the rich hire the best lawyers, and some crimes are never discovered at all. God’s judgment will have none of these flaws. Of the coming King, Isaiah says, “He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, but with righteousness he shall judge the poor” (Isaiah 11:3–4).

He knows everything. “For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14). He cannot be bribed or flattered: “God shows no partiality” (Romans 2:11). He weighs not only acts but motives: the Lord “will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart” (1 Corinthians 4:5). Nothing will be missed, exaggerated or twisted, and every person will know that the verdict is true.

For those who have been badly wronged, this is deep comfort. The case that was closed too soon, the abuse that was never believed, the cruelty no one saw: none of it is lost. If you are suffering wrong now, though, trusting God’s judgment does not mean staying silent. Get to safety, and report crimes to the authorities. God has given human courts a real task (Romans 13:1–4). His final judgment does not replace them. It completes what they cannot finish.

A day appointed, a man appointed

The Bible speaks of a definite day. When Paul spoke to the thinkers of Athens, he told them that God “commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:30–31).

Notice who the Judge is. “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), “because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27). The one who will judge the world is a man, who knows our frailty from the inside, who was tempted as we are, and who was himself unjustly tried and condemned. And God has given proof: the resurrection is the public sign that this Jesus is the appointed Judge. The empty tomb is not only a comfort; it is a summons.

Judgment now and judgment then

God’s judgments in history, the flood, Sodom, the exile, the fall of empires, are real but partial. They are previews of the final day. Even now, Paul says, God gives people over to the things they choose (Romans 1:24). But the final judgment is still to come: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27).

Why the delay? Not because God is careless, but because he is patient. “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). Every day the Judge waits is a day of mercy.

An example

A mother whose teenage daughter was killed by a drunk driver sits in court and hears a sentence that seems shockingly light. For months the bitterness eats at her. Her pastor does not tell her to stop caring about justice. He reads Genesis 18:25 with her and says that the judge in that courtroom was not the last judge. Slowly she finds she can leave the final verdict with God. It does not end her grief, but it lifts a weight she was never meant to carry.

For reflection

Why is it good news that God’s justice is part of his goodness, not opposed to it? What comfort do you find in a Judge who knows every secret and cannot be bribed? Why does it matter that the Judge is a man who was himself unjustly condemned? How should God’s patience shape the way you think about the delay of judgment?

3.title: What Jesus Taught About Hell
3.essay:
It surprises many people to learn that the strongest warnings about hell in the Bible come not from angry prophets or stern apostles, but from Jesus. The one who welcomed children, touched lepers and forgave prostitutes spoke about hell more plainly than anyone else in Scripture.

From Jesus’ own lips

The word most often translated “hell” in the New Testament is Gehenna. It appears twelve times, and eleven of them are on the lips of Jesus. The only other is in James (James 3:6). He warned that anger and contempt can make a person “liable to the hell of fire” (Matthew 5:22). He told his disciples, “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28).

Notice to whom he said it. In Luke’s Gospel the warning begins, “I tell you, my friends” (Luke 12:4). Jesus did not speak of hell to bully strangers. He spoke of it to people he loved, because he loved them.

The valley outside the city

Gehenna means “the Valley of Hinnom”, a ravine curving round the south and west of Jerusalem. It had a dark history. Two kings of Judah, Ahaz and Manasseh, burned their own sons there as offerings to false gods (2 Chronicles 28:3; 33:6). King Josiah later “defiled Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom” (2 Kings 23:10) to stop the practice. Jeremiah said it would one day be called “the Valley of Slaughter” (Jeremiah 7:32), full of the dead under God’s judgment.

So by Jesus’ day the name had become a picture of the place of final judgment. You may have heard that it was a burning rubbish dump. That idea is often repeated, but the evidence for it is late and uncertain. What is clear is that the valley stood for idolatry, the murder of the innocent, and the judgment that falls on them.

Fire and the worm

Jesus’ most searching words come in Mark 9. Better to lose a hand, a foot or an eye than “to be thrown into hell, ‘where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched’” (Mark 9:47–48). He is quoting the very last verse of Isaiah, which speaks of “the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched” (Isaiah 66:24). Isaiah sets this beside the new heavens and the new earth. There are two destinies, side by side.

Fire speaks of pain, of destruction and of the holy wrath of God against evil. The worm speaks of corruption that eats away from within; many Christian writers have seen in it a picture of a conscience that will not stop gnawing. Jesus is describing ruin, not merely pain.

Outer darkness

Jesus used another picture too: being shut out of a feast. “Many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:11–12). Inside: light, welcome, joy. Outside: darkness, grief and rage. Weeping is sorrow; gnashing of teeth is bitter anger. Neither is repentance.

Fire and darkness cannot both be literal at once, since fire gives light. That tells us these are pictures. But pictures of what? Not of something milder than the words, but of something worse than words can say. A picture is used when plain description fails.

Eternal, and away from his presence

In the parable of the sheep and the goats (see Sheep and Goats), the King says, “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). Then come the words that have shaped Christian teaching more than any others: “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). Notice too that the fire was “prepared for the devil and his angels”. Hell was not built with human beings in mind. Those who go there go where they were never meant to be.

Paul draws out what lies at the heart of it. The lost “will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). Every good thing we have ever enjoyed, light, friendship, beauty, laughter, love, came from God. Hell is to be cut off from the source of all of them. It is not that God is absent in every sense, for no one can escape him (Psalm 139:7–8). It is that his kindness is withdrawn, and only his justice remains.

What the images do not mean

Some popular ideas need correcting. Hell is not Satan’s kingdom where he rules and torments others; he is its chief prisoner (Revelation 20:10). It is not the scene of medieval paintings, with demons and pitchforks; those come from the artists, not from Jesus. It is not arbitrary: people are judged “according to what they had done” (Revelation 20:12). It is not a place where people long for God and are refused. And it is not something God delights in: “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).

An example

A fourteen-year-old at a church youth group asks her leader whether hell is “real fire”. Her leader explains that Jesus used fire and darkness as pictures, and that the reality is not less serious but more: to be shut out from God and from everything good, for ever. Then he asks her why she thinks Jesus warned his friends so often. She thinks for a moment and says, “Because he didn’t want them to go there.” She has understood the heart of it.

For reflection

Why do you think the gentlest person who ever lived spoke so often about hell? What do the pictures of fire, worm and outer darkness each teach? Why is “away from the presence of the Lord” such a terrible description? Which popular ideas about hell have you absorbed that Jesus did not teach?

4.title: Where Christians Differ
4.essay:
Christians who love the Bible and confess the same Lord have not all understood hell in the same way. This is a subject on which we should listen carefully, state other views as their holders would, and speak with humility. Here are the main positions, each at full strength.

What Christians share

First, what the historic churches agree on. God is just. Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. Sin is real and deserves judgment. Salvation is through Christ alone. The differences concern what happens to those who are not saved, and how long it lasts.

Eternal conscious punishment

This has been the main view of the church through its history: of Augustine, of the medieval church, of the Reformers, and of the great Protestant confessions, including the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession. It holds that the lost will exist for ever under God’s just punishment, conscious of their loss.

Its case rests above all on Jesus’ words: “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). The same word “eternal” describes both destinies; if the life has no end, it seems the punishment has none either. Revelation says that the devil and his allies “will be tormented day and night forever and ever” (Revelation 20:10), and of human worshippers of the beast that “they have no rest, day or night” (Revelation 14:11). Daniel speaks of some who awake “to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2), and the rich man in Jesus’ parable is conscious and in anguish (Luke 16:23–24).

Conditional immortality

Some evangelicals hold that the lost will be raised, judged and punished in proportion to their sins, and then finally destroyed, ceasing to exist. This is often called annihilationism or conditional immortality. The British pastor John Stott suggested it, tentatively, in a published dialogue in 1988. He held it cautiously and asked that it be discussed as a question of Scripture, not of feeling. Others, such as John Wenham and Edward Fudge, argued for it at length. They hold firmly to the Trinity, the cross and the authority of Scripture.

Their case deserves a fair hearing. God “alone has immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16); immortality is a gift brought to light through the gospel (2 Timothy 1:10), not a natural possession of every soul. Scripture’s most common words for the fate of the lost are death, destruction and perishing: “whoever believes in him should not perish” (John 3:16). Fire, they say, consumes. “Eternal punishment” may mean a punishment whose result is eternal, just as Christ secured “an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12) by a single act. And the smoke that rises “forever” echoes Isaiah’s picture of Edom, a land laid waste whose smoke goes up “forever” (Isaiah 34:10), a lasting sign of a judgment that is finished.

Universalism

Some have hoped that in the end all will be saved. In the early church Origen speculated about a final restoration of all things, and Gregory of Nyssa hoped for it too. In recent years some writers, including a few evangelicals and the Orthodox scholar David Bentley Hart, have argued for it openly. They point to God’s desire that “all people” be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), to his plan “to unite all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10), and to the promise that every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10–11). Surely, they ask, the love of God will not finally be defeated? Perhaps hell is a fire that purifies and the gates of the city are never shut (Revelation 21:25).

The church as a whole has not accepted this view. Uniting all things in Christ means bringing all under his rule. Every knee will bow, but not every knee willingly. And some of Jesus’ words seem impossible to square with it: of Judas he said, “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matthew 26:24), which could not be true if Judas would one day enter endless joy.

Purgatory

The Roman Catholic Church teaches purgatory. It is not a second chance for unbelievers. It is a final purification after death for those who die in God’s grace but are not yet fully purified, so that they may enter heaven. Catholics point to the ancient practice of praying for the dead, to 2 Maccabees 12 (a book they receive as Scripture), and to Paul’s words about one who “will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15).

The Reformers rejected it because it seemed to add to the finished work of Christ. “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). The dying thief was told, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). And the fire of 1 Corinthians 3 tests the work a teacher has built, not the person. The study Death, Dying & Heaven says more.

Weighing them

This commentary’s view: hell is conscious, eternal punishment. We hold it chiefly because Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence, and because Revelation speaks of torment “forever and ever”. We hold it with trembling, not with satisfaction. We honour John Stott and others who have taken the other view out of reverence for Scripture, and we grant that their arguments are serious. We reject universalism and purgatory, because Scripture does not hold out hope beyond death for those who reject Christ, nor any need for purification beyond his blood. And we confess that much about the life to come is beyond us. We know enough to warn and to plead. We do not know enough to be glib.

An example

Two friends in a home group discover that they disagree. One has read Stott and leans toward conditional immortality; the other holds the historic view. They talk it through over several weeks, Bibles open, and neither wholly convinces the other. But both notice that the conversation has made them pray more earnestly for their unbelieving relatives. Whatever hell is, they agree, it is the most serious thing in the world to be lost.

For reflection

Why is it important to state other views as their holders would? Which arguments for conditional immortality do you find most weighty, and how would you answer them? Why is universalism so attractive, and what makes it hard to hold from the words of Jesus? How can Christians disagree on this subject without losing urgency or love?

5.title: Is It Fair?
5.essay:
Even when we accept what Jesus taught, a question lingers. Is it fair? Can a finite life of wrongdoing deserve an endless punishment? What about those who never heard of Christ? These are not questions to be dismissed. Scripture does not answer every one of them fully, but it says more than we might expect.

Not everyone the same

We often picture hell as a single sentence handed out equally to all who fall short. Jesus did not teach that. A servant “who knew his master’s will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:47–48).

He told Capernaum, a town that had seen many of his miracles, that “it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you” (Matthew 11:24). God “will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6). The Judge weighs the light a person had and the motives of the heart. No one will suffer one degree more than they deserve. And no one will leave that courtroom thinking the verdict unjust.

Given what they chose

C. S. Lewis made a point that has helped many. In The Great Divorce he said, in effect, that in the end there are only two kinds of people: those who say to God, your will be done, and those to whom God finally says, your will be done. Elsewhere he suggested that the doors of hell are locked from the inside.

There is real truth here. Jesus said, “this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil” (John 3:19). Even now God gives people over to what they insist on (Romans 1:24). Hell is, in part, God giving people the life without him that they wanted: a self curved in on itself, with nothing left but itself.

But Scripture says more than Lewis’s line alone. Hell is also a sentence. The King says, “Depart from me” (Matthew 25:41). It is not only what sinners choose; it is what sin deserves. Both are true: the lost are not dragged away from a God they love, and they are justly condemned by a God they have wronged.

The size of the offence

Why should sin deserve so much? Part of the answer lies in whom it is against. The same act can carry very different weight depending on its target. To kick a tin can is nothing; to kick a dog is cruel; to kick a child is a crime. The weight of a wrong grows with the worth of the one wronged. Christian thinkers such as Anselm and Jonathan Edwards argued that sin against a God of infinite worth and goodness carries a weight beyond our measuring. David, after his adultery and murder, said, “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4). He had wronged others terribly, yet he saw that the deepest offence was against God.

And sin is not only a list of separate acts. It is the heart turning from the God who made it and loves it, to worship created things instead (Romans 1:21–25). We do not easily feel its weight, because we are the ones who did it.

Those who never heard

This is the question many find hardest. Here we must speak carefully and humbly. Scripture teaches that God has made himself known to every person through creation: “his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived… So they are without excuse” (Romans 1:20). Every conscience bears some witness to his law (Romans 2:14–15). So no one will be condemned for failing to believe a gospel they never heard. People are judged for sin against the light they had: “all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Romans 2:12).

Yet creation and conscience leave people without excuse; they do not give a way of salvation. “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). That is why Paul asks, “how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard?” (Romans 10:14), and why the church is sent. Some Christians, called inclusivists, hope that God may save some through Christ without their hearing of him; this commentary does not find that taught in Scripture. The studies Missions & the Nations and Evangelism (One Way, Held with Humility) take this further.

And what of infants and those who die before they can understand? Here grieving parents may rest their little ones in the hands of a God of real mercy, as Death, Dying & Heaven (Grieving with Hope) explains.

In the end, where Scripture is silent we can rest in two things. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29). And the Judge of all the earth will do what is just.

The question turned around

The more we look, the more the question turns around. We begin by asking, “How can it be fair that anyone is lost?” Scripture leads us to a more startling question: “How can it be fair that anyone is saved?” If we deserve judgment, how can a just God welcome us? That is the question the next chapter answers.

An example

A young woman whose family came from a remote region asks her pastor about her great-grandparents, who died before any missionary arrived. He tells her that God judges by the light people had, that he will do nothing unjust, and that she can leave them with him. Then he asks her gently about the cousins still living there. A year later she is studying to translate Scripture into her family’s language.

For reflection

How does Luke 12:47–48 change your picture of judgment? What is helpful in Lewis’s idea that hell is God giving people what they chose, and what does it leave out? Why does the worth of the one wronged affect the weight of a wrong? How should the question of those who never heard shape your praying and giving?

6.title: The Cross: Judgment Taken for Us
6.essay:
The judgment of God has already fallen once in full, at a particular place, on a particular afternoon, just outside the walls of Jerusalem. The day of judgment that every human being faces came early for one man. And it came for us.

The problem only God could solve

How can a just God welcome the guilty? A judge who simply let criminals go would be corrupt. If God overlooked sin he would cease to be just. If he punished every sinner, no one would be saved.

Paul shows how God did both. He “put forward” Christ “as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness… so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25–26). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away wrath by bearing it. God did not lower his standard to save us. He met it himself.

The cup

The night before he died, Jesus fell on his face in Gethsemane and prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). What cup? The prophets had spoken of “the cup of his wrath” (Isaiah 51:17), and Revelation pictures the lost drinking “the wine of God’s wrath, poured full strength into the cup of his anger” (Revelation 14:10). Jesus was not shrinking from pain as a coward does. He was facing the cup poured out for sinners, and he drank it to the bottom so that we never will.

Darkness at noon

On the cross, Mark tells us, “there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, ‘Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?’ which means, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’” (Mark 15:33–34).

Remember Jesus’ own picture of hell: outer darkness, shut out from the feast, away from the presence of the Lord. Now the light of the sun fails at midday, and the Son, who had known the Father’s love from all eternity, cries out as one forsaken. The Trinity was not broken apart; the Father never stopped loving his Son, and loved him precisely for laying down his life (John 10:17). And even in the darkness Jesus still says, “My God.” But in his human soul he endured the forsakenness that sin deserves. He went into the outer darkness so that we could come in to the feast.

The Apostles’ Creed says that Christ “descended into hell”. Christians have read that line in different ways. John Calvin took it to mean, above all, that on the cross Christ suffered in his soul the dread and anguish of a man condemned and forsaken by God. The Heidelberg Catechism draws the pastoral comfort: in my deepest trials I may be sure that Christ, by his unspeakable anguish, has set me free from the anguish of hell. Jesus went to the place of forsakenness so that his people would never be forsaken.

The curse carried

The New Testament says it again and again. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Isaiah had seen it centuries before: “he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities… and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:5–6).

The Judge of all the earth stood in the court of Pontius Pilate and was condemned. The one who will judge the world was judged in its place. The Person & Work of Christ (The Cross: Christ Our Substitute) explains this more fully.

No condemnation

For everyone who trusts in Christ, the day of judgment has, in the deepest sense, already happened. It was moved forward to Good Friday, and the sentence was carried out on Jesus. That is why he can say, “whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24). That is why Paul can say, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and ask, “Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died… who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34). Justice is not set aside. Justice has been done. It would be unjust for God to demand payment twice.

The measure of his love

If hell is a small thing, then the cross is a small thing. If what Jesus bore was only a little discomfort, his love was only a little love. But if hell is what Jesus said it is, then the cross is greater than we can take in. He took into himself, in those hours of darkness, what we would never have come to the end of. “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10).

The doctrine of hell, rightly understood, does not make the gospel darker. It shows us how bright it is. The Judge we feared has become the Saviour we love, and the one thing we could never pay has been paid in full. “It is finished” (John 19:30).

An example

An old man in hospital tells his pastor he is afraid to die. He was a hard man for most of his life. “I know what I deserve,” he says. The pastor does not tell him he was not so bad. He reads Isaiah 53 and Romans 8:1 and says, “Yes, you know what you deserve. Now look at who took it.” The old man is quiet for a long time. Then he asks to hear the verses again.

For reflection

How does Romans 3:25–26 show that God is both just and merciful at the cross? What does the cry “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34) tell you about what Jesus bore? Why does a smaller view of hell lead to a smaller view of the cross? What would it mean for you to believe that your day of judgment has already been carried out on Christ?

7.title: Living in the Light of Judgment
7.essay:
The truth about judgment is not meant to sit in a book. It is meant to change how we speak to our neighbours, how we face our own failures, how we grieve, and how we sleep at night. Rightly held, it produces not dread but urgency, humility, compassion and deep peace.

Urgency, with tears

Paul wrote, “knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others” (2 Corinthians 5:11), and a few lines later, “We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). If judgment is real, then the gospel is not a lifestyle option. It is rescue.

But the urgency of the Bible is never cold. Paul said of his unbelieving kinsmen, “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (Romans 9:2). There is a story that Andrew Bonar once told his friend Robert Murray M’Cheyne that he had preached on the judgment of the wicked, and M’Cheyne asked whether he had been able to preach it with tenderness. That is the right question. We are not judges looking down on the guilty. We are pardoned criminals telling others where pardon can be found. Anger, scorn and superiority have no place in it. Tears do.

In practice this means praying by name for people who do not know Christ, speaking of him plainly, and being honest about judgment when friends ask, neither hiding it nor using it as a club.

Confidence for believers

For those who trust Christ, judgment day need not be a terror. John says that love is perfected among us “so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment… There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:17–18).

Believers will still stand before Christ: “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body” (2 Corinthians 5:10). But this is not a second trial in which our salvation hangs in the balance. Our lives will be revealed and our works, imperfect as they are, rewarded by grace. The study Good Works says more. We will stand there as children before a Father, not as criminals before a court.

Grief for those we love

The hardest place this doctrine touches is the heart of someone who loves an unbeliever, or who has lost one. A son who walked away from the faith; a father who died without any sign of turning to Christ.

While they live, keep praying and keep loving. God has saved many after decades of prayer. When they have died, we must not pretend to certainties we do not have, either way. We do not know all that passed between a dying person and God in the last hours; the thief on the cross was saved at the very end (Luke 23:42–43). Yet neither may we invent hopes Scripture does not give.

What we can do is rest where Abraham rested: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). On that day we will not find his judgment cruel. We will see that he did right in everything, with a fullness of knowledge and love we lack now. And he has promised that he “will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). We can trust the one who wept over Jerusalem.

When the fear will not let go

Some believers live under a constant dread of hell. They fear they have committed the unpardonable sin, or that their faith is not real, or that one more failure will cast them off. Pastors have long noticed that those who are tormented by the fear of having committed the unforgivable sin are the very ones who have not, for that sin is a settled, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, not a fear of having grieved him.

If this is you, hear Jesus: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Your safety rests on his grip on you, not your grip on him (John 10:28). The study Assurance of Salvation and the study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation may help.

Such fears can also become a lasting struggle, sometimes linked to anxiety or to a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder called scrupulosity. Then do not try to carry it alone. Speak to your pastor and ask for a biblical counsellor, through your church or an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the United States or Biblical Counselling UK. A good counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up as well, because body and soul affect each other, and medical treatment is no failure of faith. God’s Word is sufficient for the care of the soul, and a wise counsellor will open it with you patiently. And if fear or despair ever brings thoughts of ending your life, please tell someone today: call the emergency services or a crisis line, or go to a trusted person and say it out loud.

An example

A young mother lies awake most nights convinced she has crossed a line with God and is lost. An older woman from church notices, begins meeting with her, and helps her find a biblical counsellor, who asks her to see her doctor too. Week by week they read John 6 and Romans 8 together. Months later the fears still come at times, but she has learned to answer them: “He said he would never cast me out.”

The Judge who was judged

Every human being will one day stand before Jesus Christ. For some it will be the most terrible moment of their existence; for others, the moment they have longed for. The difference will not be how good they were, but whether they came to him.

And he still invites. “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The Judge of all the earth has stretched out the hands that were pierced for us. The last word of the Bible on this subject is not a threat but an invitation: “let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (Revelation 22:17).

For reflection

How can you speak of judgment with both urgency and tenderness? What difference does 1 John 4:17–18 make to the way you think about your own day of judgment? Is there someone you love whom you need to entrust to the Judge of all the earth? If fear of hell troubles you, who could you talk to this week?
